## Introduction

A well known ecogeographical pattern describes the relationship between temperature variation and body size. This association is known as Bergmann's rule .

Two of the main responses of organisms to climate change are phenological changes and geographical range shifts [@parmesan_globally_2003]. Yet, a third response of organisms to global warming is increasingly being observed, the shrinkage of bodies [@teplitsky_climate_2014; @sheridan_shrinking_2011; @gardner_declining_2011]. Body size shrinkage due to climate change has been hypothesized to be a consequence of ecological or evolutionary processes [@ozgul_dynamics_2009]. The ecological hypothesis posits that climate change influences trophic interactions, thus leading to a reduction in body size.

Changes in temperature can result in temperature-dependent or -independent mechanisms that influence body size [reviewed in @gardner_declining_2011]. Among temperature-independent mechanisms, decreases in food availability caused by habitat loss or fragmentation may lead to the reduction of body size [@schmidt_concomitant_2005]. Thus, limiting juveniles access to resources could lead to smaller adult body size [@teplitsky_bergmanns_2008; @rode_reduced_2010]. Reductions in body size have been attributed to genetic microevolutionary responses to warming; smaller individuals dissipate heat better than larger individuals due to the larger ratio between surface:volume of their bodies [*e.g.*, Bergmann's rule, @teplitsky_climate_2014].[^1]

[^1]: I think that this paragraph is not necessary. Talk only about the ecological consequences.

### Research Question

Here, we will conduct a large scale comparative phylogenetic analysis of Neotropical passerines that inhabit the Brazilian Atlantic Forest to investigate whether temporal changes in climate variables are associated with body size changes.
